messages.subject: modeling subsets of all variables
messages.subject_clean: modeling subsets of all variables
messages.body_plain:
I am using the pcount function and I have 5 variables (some continuous, some categorical) that may influence detection probability for 9 species of birds.  I want to model which variables give the best model for detection probability.  Is there a way to easily model and compare all subsets/combinations of my variables, or do I have to write every single combination out separately?

Detection Variables:
observer
date
time
visit
wind

messages.subject_clean: modeling subsets of all variables
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jason,

If you want to compare different models, you can use some of the functionalities of the AICcmodavg package (model selection, multimodel inference, check GOF), as Marc Kéry suggested. However, you will have to write out each model that you want to compare. I intentionally did not include any functions to automagically generate all possible combinations of variables to steer users away from "fishing expeditions" and keep the number of models down. It is important to think about each model you want to include in your candidate model set and check the output of each model for potential problems (e.g., lack of convergence, parameters on boundaries, ill conditioning). Just looking at the resulting model selection table to see which model is best can be misleading.

Hope it helps,

Marc

messages.subject: Estimating detection probability with categorical covariates
messages.subject_clean: Estimating detection probability with categorical covariates
messages.body_plain:
Dear Unmarked Community,

I am using a pcountOpen model with 4 continuous and 1 categorical covariate in the detection model to estimate the effects of those covariates on detection probability. My question concerns how to treat the categorical covariate when estimating the effects of the continuous ones on p. I have set the covariate of interest as a sequence of numbers between its max and min scaled values, set other continuous covariates at their mean values, and the categorical covariate at one of the three possible levels.  Code below:

>fm_best <- pcountOpen(~1, ~1, ~1, ~Temp + I(Temp^2) + TAS + I(TAS^2)+ Topo + DOY + MRain  , cnti.umf, K=70, mixture = "P", dynamics = "trend", se = TRUE)

>topos<-as.character(c("valley floor","rocky slope","bajada"))

>new.dat12<-data.frame(TAS=seq(-2.3467, 3.197,length=32), Temp=0,MRain=0,DOY=0, Topo=factor("valley floor",levels=c(unique(topos))))

>TAS.dat12<-predict(fm_best,type="det",newdata=new.dat12,appendData=T)

I have had no trouble predicting p like this but am unsure if I should be computing average p for each continuous covariate among all levels of the categorical covariate (e.g., different Topo levels).

 (1) Is it best to average the 3 predicted values of p at each possible levels (in other words, should I use the output of rowMeans(Avg) as seen below)?

            >DOY.M=seq(-3.163,2.598,length=100)

>new.datDOY<-data.frame(DOY=DOY.M,MRain=0,TAS=0,Temp=0, Topo=factor("valley floor",levels=c(unique(topos))))

>DOY.dat<-predict(fm_best,type="det",newdata=new.datDOY,appendData=T)

>new.datDOY2<-data.frame(DOY=DOY.M,MRain=0,TAS=0,Temp=0, Topo=factor("rocky slope",levels=c(unique(topos))))

>DOY.dat2<-predict(fm_best,type="det",newdata=new.datDOY2,appendData=T)

>new.datDOY3<-data.frame(DOY=DOY.M,MRain=0,TAS=0,Temp=0, Topo=factor("bajada",levels=c(unique(topos))))

>DOY.dat3<-predict(fm_best,type="det",newdata=new.datDOY3,appendData=T)

>Avg=cbind(DOY.dat[,1],DOY.dat2[,1],DOY.dat3[,1])

>rowMeans(Avg)

 (2) If so, how would I calculate the CIs? In Fig. 2 of Kery (2009), “Trend estimation in populations with imperfect detection”, predictions of detection probability were calculated by averaging over the categorical covariates, but how were the 95% CI calculated?

 Any help on this would be appreciated!

Charlotte

Dear Charlotte,

I think I would simply refit the model without the factor and then you're fine with the predict() function.

In the paper you cite we used BUGS and one of the greatest things about a Bayesian MCMC-based analysis is that you can forget about the delta method: getting SE's and other measures of estimation uncertainty are coming for free.

Kind regards  --- Marc

messages.body_plain:
Dear Charlotte,

I actually meant remove TOPO from the model, i.e., refit the model without the factor, and not simply removing if from the data frame (which I am not even sure why this works at all). I think that this will result in predictions for the continuous covariates that are automatically averaged over the effects of the TOPO factor (in the same sense as a model always implicitly averages over any factor/covariate that is not in it).

One comment about forming predictions, which is notoriously confusing when transformations are involved. Here is how I do it in a way that I get less easily confused.

(1)    I first compute the "prediction covariate", which contains values in the range of the continuous covariate over which I want to predict:

TAS.original <- seq(-2.3, 3.2, length = 100)             # More values result in smoother plots

(2)    Then, I transform the values of the prediction covariate in the exact same way as I did in my analysis:

TAS <- (TAS.original – mean.TAS) / sd.TAS       # Where mean.TAS and sd.TAS are computed from your actual data

(3)    Then, I predict using the TAS covariate (which is standardised as in the analysis), i.e., I create the prediction data frame and use it for prediction:

new.dat <- data.frame(TAS=TAS, Temp=0,MRain=0,DOY=0)

predi.p.for.tas <- predict(fm_best, type="det",newdata=new.dat,appendData=T)

(4)    Finally, when plotting, I use the original (unstandardised) values of TAS, e.g.

plot(TAS.original, predi.p.for.tas[1,])

Kind regards  ---- Marc

Dear Charlotte,

I actually meant remove TOPO from the model, i.e., refit the model without the factor, and not simply removing if from the data frame (which I am not even sure why this works at all). I think that this will result in predictions for the continuous covariates that are automatically averaged over the effects of the TOPO factor (in the same sense as a model always implicitly averages over any factor/covariate that is not in it).

One comment about forming predictions, which is notoriously confusing when transformations are involved. Here is how I do it in a way that I get less easily confused.

(1)    I first compute the "prediction covariate", which contains values in the range of the continuous covariate over which I want to predict:

TAS.original <- seq(-2.3, 3.2, length = 100)             # More values result in smoother plots

(2)    Then, I transform the values of the prediction covariate in the exact same way as I did in my analysis:

TAS <- (TAS.original – mean.TAS) / sd.TAS       # Where mean.TAS and sd.TAS are computed from your actual data

(3)    Then, I predict using the TAS covariate (which is standardised as in the analysis), i.e., I create the prediction data frame and use it for prediction:

new.dat <- data.frame(TAS=TAS, Temp=0,MRain=0,DOY=0)

predi.p.for.tas <- predict(fm_best, type="det",newdata=new.dat,appendData=T)

(4)    Finally, when plotting, I use the original (unstandardised) values of TAS, e.g.

plot(TAS.original, predi.p.for.tas[1,])

Kind regards  ---- Marc

messages.body_plain:
Dear Marc and unmarked users,

We are facing a similar issue and are wondering if found advice for your earlier post?

A tutorial for the ordinal package suggests that condition numbers of 10^4 or 10^6 indicate ill-defined models. (Page 4 of http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ordinal/vignettes/clm_tutorial.pdf)

Could the difference in condition number value described as problematic be due to variation in how the condition number is calculated? Some methods appear to take the log while others do not.

Thank you,
Lydia

On Wednesday, August 20, 2014 at 11:14:22 AM UTC-4, Kery Marc wrote:
> Dear colleagues,
>
> we are fitting dynamic occupancy models to a relatively sparse data set (80 sites, about 15 years, 3 reps per year). With easily 10 covariates to choose from (not including YEAR), the model complexity/information content ratio becomes an issue. For instance, we have lots of boundary estimates and very large SE's, indicating numerical problems.
>
> As a further indication of numerical problems, I thought we could use the condition number, which is the ratio of the largest to the smallest eigenvalue of either the Hessian matrix or the variance-covariance matrix (and whether it's the former or the latter is exactly my first question):
>
> max(eigen(hessian(fitted.model.object))$values)/min(eigen(hessian(fitted.model.object))$values)
>
> According to a Wikipedia entry, values greater than 30 indicate problems. However, we get values that are several orders of magnitude greater than that even for models for which the MLE point estimates and SE's seem to look fine.
>
> Does anybody have experience in that and could give some advice ?
>
> Thanks and kind regards  --- Marc

messages.body_plain:
Hi Richard,

I am bringing back up an old thread, but I noticed in the source code that AIC for colext() is now calculating AIC and not AICc (per Chad's comment) and I know that I can calculate AICc by hand, but one suggestion to add to your already large to-do list would be to give the option of picking what type of model selection criteria to use (AIC vs. AICc). Based on Anderson's suggestion of using AICc in practice I would think a lot of people would like the option of using it conveniently within colext() and unmarked.

I may have missed this option and if I did I am sorry.

Thanks for the hard work you put into unmarked. Its a great package and the reason I suggest this idea is that I really like the modSel() function and being able to export the tables so quickly. Super convenient!

Cheers.

Travis Gallo
Ph.D. Candidate
Sustainability Leadership Fellow - School of Global Environmental Sustainability
Department of Fish, Wildlife and Conservation Biology
Colorado State University

>
>
> which I guess is AICc assuming that the sample size is equal to the number of sites. I will fix this so that it returns AIC to be

> logLik(someModel)
>
>
> Richard

> > not AIC. I looked at previous threads on the google group, and I did
> > not notice any resolution on this issue. It’s not a big deal, I can
> > calculate either AICc or AIC given the -2log and number of parameters.
> > But what is it calculating; the output calls it AIC?
> > The example below is from when I run a constant model and a “habitat”
> > model with n=47. Notice that 261.5+(2*4) does not equal 270.5 (it
> > equals 269.5) but when we account for the 47 sites and calculate AICc,
> > 261.5+2*4(47/(47-4-1) , we get 270.452380… which is very similar to
> > the AIC value in the table. This is even clearer when there are more
> > parameters (habitat model). I have double checked this table to model@
> > AIC and I get the same results.
> >
> >                                          Model Converge -2logLik K
> > AIC DeltaAIC     w
> > 1 ~habitat , ~habitat , ~habitat , ~1        0   -249.8      7
> > 266.7      0.0 0.869
> > 2                   ~1 , ~1 , ~1 , ~1              0   -261.5      4
> > 270.5      3.8 0.131
> >
> >
> > Chad Hockenbary
> > GRA
> > Montana State University

Travis,

Defining the sample size for occupancy-type models is not
straightforward.

In AICcmodavg, if you want AICc for unmarkedFit models, it uses the
number of sites as the sample size:

AICc(mod, second.order = TRUE, nobs = NULL) returns AICc using the
number of sites as sample size. You may change it to another value if
you prefer by specifying it in the "nobs" argument.

You can get "classic" AIC like so:
AICc(mod, second.order = FALSE) returns AIC.

Note that "second.order" and "nobs" arguments are also present in the
model selection and multimodel inference functions of the package. For
instance, see ?aictab, ?modavgPred, ?modavg, for examples of their use.

Best,

Marc

messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] descritizing camera data for occupancy analysis
messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] descritizing camera data for occupancy analysis
messages.body_plain:
Dear Robin,

if you discretize and analyse using a standard occupancy model, then you typically lose information, whenever more than a single detection per occasion gets subsumed into a single '1' in the resulting history. Viewed from this angle, it would be best to discretize finely so that you never have more than a single detection per occasion. On the other hand, this may lead to very large data sets (lots of occasions) and moreover, there may be serial dependence, i.e., neighbouring occasions may not be independent samples from the underlying presence/absence process. This is a problem that you would have to deal with by adoping more complex occupancy models, see Hines et al. (tigers on trails paper, 2010) and recent follow-up paper for dynamic occupancy. These models have been implemented in PRESENCE (not sure about MARK). Note that independence or lack thereof in space (as for transect-based sampling) is very similar or identical to that in time (as for your camera-trap data).

Some would argue that discretisation of measurements made on a continuous process is always a bad idea and that you should directly model a continuous detection process, in space or in time. This typically leads to Poisson process models, which in the context of occupancy estimation have been introduced by Gurutzeta Guillera Arroita (GGA) (papers in JABES, MEE and elsewhere). The simplest such models assumes independence in space or time. The individual detections can be aggregated into a detection frequency per transect or per camera and some total time interval, say C_i for the number of detections at trap or transect i.

Then, you can specify the following variant of occupancy model, which has a Poisson instead of a Binomial description of the observation process:

z_i ~ Bernoulli(psi)              # Presence/absence (z) is like a coin flip
C_i ~ Poisson(z_i * lambda_i) # lambda is detection rate, i.e., the expected number of detections given that a site is occupied.

You can model pattern in occupancy probability by logit(psi_i) = some linear model and those in the detection frequency by log(lambda_i) = some linear model, exactly as in a GLM (this model is the combination of a logistic regression for occupancy and a Poisson regression for the number of detections).

This model can easily be fitted in BUGS. Note that for this model, a single replicate is enough (there is no j). Also note that one would usually have an offset in the Poisson part of the model, to account for unequal length (of time or transect) of observation.

If you can assume independence, then this seems to be a very useful model. If you don't have independence (for instance, some aggregation of detection in time or space), then this autocorrelation ought to be modelled and you must model the individual detections. One conceptually simple way of doing so is by imagining two latent processes underlying the measured detections, between which there are switches with some probability. GGA have lately developed such a 2MMPP model (a 2-state Markov-modulated point process model --- try to say this a couple of times quickly ....). She has code in Matlab, but I think not (yet) for any language that is widely spoken in ecology, such as R or BUGS.

Kind regards  --  Marc

btw: the need for a (much) more complex model for un-discretized camera-trap detections in the case of serial dependence may provide one motivation for discretisation and modeling of aggregated data. In that way you may get rid of dependence and hence be able to use a simpler model (or do estimation at all, if you don't know how to fit the more complex model). Stats is like real life, so full with trade-offs  ......

messages.body_plain:
Marc
Thanks for a superb overview of the issues. Almost a publishable unit!
I wonder if you didn't shoot yourself in the foot with your addendum - doesn't aggregation just shift the problem from 'independence' to 'overdispersion'?
On 2MMPP - I described Gurutzeta's original paper as an 'instant classic'. I adapted her (privately provided) code for R and C at the time and have it somewhere. I became a bit disillusioned with 2MMPP as a way of modelling cue production (singing) by birds - it seemed to have limited ability to match the distribution of total cue number when birds sing intermittently because birds sing in non-Poisson bouts. The same limitation may apply elsewhere.
Murray

Sent: Saturday, 17 January 2015 11:33 p.m.

Subject: RE: [unmarked] descritizing camera data for occupancy analysis

btw: the need for a (much) more complex model for un-discretized camera-trap detections in the case of serial dependence may provide one motivation for discretisation and modeling of aggregated data. In that way you may get rid of dependence and hence be able to use a simpler model (or do estimation at all, if you don't know how to fit the more complex model). Stats is like real life, so full with trade-offs  ......

Regards  -- Marc

From: unma...@googlegroups.com [unma...@googlegroups.com] on behalf of Kery Marc [marc...@vogelwarte.ch]
Sent: 17 January 2015 11:22
To: unma...@googlegroups.com
Subject: RE: [unmarked] descritizing camera data for occupancy analysis

Dear Robin,

if you discretize and analyse using a standard occupancy model, then you typically lose information, whenever more than a single detection per occasion gets subsumed into a single '1' in the resulting history. Viewed from this angle, it would be best to discretize finely so that you never have more than a single detection per occasion. On the other hand, this may lead to very large data sets (lots of occasions) and moreover, there may be serial dependence, i.e., neighbouring occasions may not be independent samples from the underlying presence/absence process. This is a problem that you would have to deal with by adoping more complex occupancy models, see Hines et al. (tigers on trails paper, 2010) and recent follow-up paper for dynamic occupancy. These models have been implemented in PRESENCE (not sure about MARK). Note that independence or lack thereof in space (as for transect-based sampling) is very similar or identical to that in time (as for your camera-trap data).

Some would argue that discretisation of measurements made on a continuous process is always a bad idea and that you should directly model a continuous detection process, in space or in time. This typically leads to Poisson process models, which in the context of occupancy estimation have been introduced by Gurutzeta Guillera Arroita (GGA) (papers in JABES, MEE and elsewhere). The simplest such models assumes independence in space or time. The individual detections can be aggregated into a detection frequency per transect or per camera and some total time interval, say C_i for the number of detections at trap or transect i.

Then, you can specify the following variant of occupancy model, which has a Poisson instead of a Binomial description of the observation process:

z_i ~ Bernoulli(psi)              # Presence/absence (z) is like a coin flip
C_i ~ Poisson(z_i * lambda_i) # lambda is detection rate, i.e., the expected number of detections given that a site is occupied.

You can model pattern in occupancy probability by logit(psi_i) = some linear model and those in the detection frequency by log(lambda_i) = some linear model, exactly as in a GLM (this model is the combination of a logistic regression for occupancy and a Poisson regression for the number of detections).

This model can easily be fitted in BUGS. Note that for this model, a single replicate is enough (there is no j). Also note that one would usually have an offset in the Poisson part of the model, to account for unequal length (of time or transect) of observation.

If you can assume independence, then this seems to be a very useful model. If you don't have independence (for instance, some aggregation of detection in time or space), then this autocorrelation ought to be modelled and you must model the individual detections. One conceptually simple way of doing so is by imagining two latent processes underlying the measured detections, between which there are switches with some probability. GGA have lately developed such a 2MMPP model (a 2-state Markov-modulated point process model --- try to say this a couple of times quickly ....). She has code in Matlab, but I think not (yet) for any language that is widely spoken in ecology, such as R or BUGS.

Kind regards  --  Marc

messages.body_plain:
Hi groups.
I have read through the posts and tried to run chisq as well as N.mixgof in order to find whether my models are fit the data. I don't know what I am doing wrong, but when I run the code (below) it takes half an hour to run and it returns all NA...

Please help me. I would like to know whether there is no evidence for lack of fit in my models.

#chisq code
chisq <- function(fm) {
  observed <- getY(umf)  ##umf is my data with covariates
  expected <- fitted(fm) ## fm is my model
  sum((observed - expected)^2 / expected) # Chisquared
}
pbfm<- parboot(fm, statistic = chisq, nsim = 1000, report=1)
pbfm
fm

pbfm16<- parboot(fm16, statistic = chisq, nsim = 1000, report=1)
pbfm16

Thanks.
Carole

  notna<- !is.na <http://is.na>(observed)

 sum(resid)
}

messages.body_plain:
Thanks Murray for sharing your experience with the 2MMPP model, and thanks Marc for distilling the Gurutzeta papers (and your touch of enlightening life philosophy :)

I gather from this list serve (and from a cross post on the yahoo  camera trapping list serve) that a succinct answer to my question of whether there was some published recommendations is: no, not much published... except for the general recommendations to NOT descritize continuous data, both in the occupancy literature (Gurutzeta) and S(E)CR literature (Borchers et al. 2014 MEE). I suppose the best way to take this advice when still chopping up continuous data is to chop it up as fine as possible (while still considering the auto-correlation issues if possible). Your point, Marc about issues with actually being able to estimate occupancy when data is chopped up very finely is well taken; I have had issues in unmarked (the usual Hessian error) when camera data was descritize a little too finely, but that goes away when collapsing data, even just a little bit. Switching to BUGS may avoid this error though, but then my simulations become too unwieldily.

Thanks for your thoughts!
Robin

messages.body_plain:
hi Robin, Marc, Murray, et al:

 This is a really good discussion of an important issue.

 I wanted to add my 2 cents worth on the issue of "to aggregate or not" -- I think for most camera trapping studies of carnivores it is pointless to try to model the continuous time data because often the very short term "visits" are almost completely dependent and those detections are not informative about the important parameters of the model.  e.g., a tiger will go back and forth along a trail segment 10 times in an hour or two, even a minute or two apart.  This is why I think using a nightly sample interval makes sense (and also it's a natural period of activity for most species).  Of course there is still potentially dependence from one night to the next but this is well modeled in many cases with a behavioral reponse.

  I make the same argument in attempting to model scat detections of some species. Many carnivores use latrines or similar high density areas and the actual rate of scatting on latrines is essentially irrelevant unless you're studying behavior.

regards
andy

messages.body_plain:
I agree strongly with Andy on this - the key point being to pick a time unit that we expect for biological reasons to yield plausibly independent data. For the remaining dependence, presumably you mean a Markovian (transient) behavioural response rather than the conventional permanent one of Otis et al. Mb.

Also, re-stating what may be already obvious and well documented: If your (nightly) observations are independent (i.e. Bernoulli trials) and you don't want to model changing detection probability over time then it is mathematically equivalent to model their aggregate as binomial (i.e. to model the sum across occasions). Can save time.

Since I mentioned 2-MMPP: I have found a 3/4-documented R package I wrote that fits this to continuous data from multiple sites for occupancy (0/1), Poisson and negative binomial N (cf Royle and Nichols). If anyone wants this they can contact me (I won't be putting it on CRAN).

Murray

messages.body_plain:
I think the issue has been summarized really well so far but I would like to add a few things based on my experience with camera trap data and occupancy models. While correlation can be an issue on a short time scale (1-2 days) overdispersion of the data is often a bigger issue, especially for abundant species and species with small home ranges. Camera traps are often run over long periods of time (e.g. 60 to 90 days) so that you can potentially end up with a large number of detections. For some species in our dataset the number of days a species was detected at a camera can range from 1 to 35 out of 60 sampling days. This heterogeneity among cameras can lead to a poor model fit. Generally we found that the Royle-Nichols model improves fit but even then there is too much overdispersion when using one day as a sampling period. Pooling the data over 5 or 6 days helps bringing those large numbers down while little affecting the low numbers. So loosing information can be helpful. So far I had little success with modeling the overdispersion using a negative binomial or a Poisson log-normal model. Using a Poisson detection model instead of a Binomial as suggested by Marc did not affect model fit either.

Overdispersion is less of an issue for carnivores with large home ranges. Those species cover large areas and spend little time near a single camera. Ungulates or smaller mammals on the other hand can can pass by a camera almost daily in some cases. Some of the differences among cameras can be addressed by covariates such as on/off trail or habitat type but we found that a lot of the variation can not be explained. It is easy to imagine that if a camera is close to an individuals home range center we would get more detections while if the camera is at the edge of a home range we get fewer detections, which is exactly what the SECR models assume. Cameras can also unintentionally be placed close to an important food source, denn, travel path etc. which increases the number of detections compared to other cameras. These detections are not necessarily correlated in time.

So my suggestion would be to try to model  your data with a Royle-Nichols model with 1 day as a sampling occasion and the assess model fit. If the model does not fit then I would pool data over several days.

Regards,

Mathias

>  This is a really good discussion of an important issue.
>
>  I wanted to add my 2 cents worth on the issue of "to aggregate or not" -- I think for most camera trapping studies of carnivores it is pointless to try to model the continuous time data because often the very short term "visits" are almost completely dependent and those detections are not informative about the important parameters of the model.  e.g., a tiger will go back and forth along a trail segment 10 times in an hour or two, even a minute or two apart.  This is why I think using a nightly sample interval makes sense (and also it's a natural period of activity for most species).  Of course there is still potentially dependence from one night to the next but this is well modeled in many cases with a behavioral reponse.
>
>   I make the same argument in attempting to model scat detections of some species. Many carnivores use latrines or similar high density areas and the actual rate of scatting on latrines is essentially irrelevant unless you're studying behavior.
>
> regards
> andy

> > > Dear Robin,
> > >
> > > if you discretize and analyse using a standard occupancy model, then you typically lose information, whenever more than a single detection per occasion gets subsumed into a single '1' in the resulting history. Viewed from this angle, it would be best to discretize finely so that you never have more than a single detection per occasion. On the other hand, this may lead to very large data sets (lots of occasions) and moreover, there may be serial dependence, i.e., neighbouring occasions may not be independent samples from the underlying presence/absence process. This is a problem that you would have to deal with by adoping more complex occupancy models, see Hines et al. (tigers on trails paper, 2010) and recent follow-up paper for dynamic occupancy. These models have been implemented in PRESENCE (not sure about MARK). Note that independence or lack thereof in space (as for transect-based sampling) is very similar or identical to that in time (as for your camera-trap data).
> > >
> > > Some would argue that discretisation of measurements made on a continuous process is always a bad idea and that you should directly model a continuous detection process, in space or in time. This typically leads to Poisson process models, which in the context of occupancy estimation have been introduced by Gurutzeta Guillera Arroita (GGA) (papers in JABES, MEE and elsewhere). The simplest such models assumes independence in space or time. The individual detections can be aggregated into a detection frequency per transect or per camera and some total time interval, say C_i for the number of detections at trap or transect i.
> > >
> > > Then, you can specify the following variant of occupancy model, which has a Poisson instead of a Binomial description of the observation process:
> > >
> > > z_i ~ Bernoulli(psi)              # Presence/absence (z) is like a coin flip
> > > C_i ~ Poisson(z_i * lambda_i) # lambda is detection rate, i.e., the expected number of detections given that a site is occupied.
> > >
> > > You can model pattern in occupancy probability by logit(psi_i) = some linear model and those in the detection frequency by log(lambda_i) = some linear model, exactly as in a GLM (this model is the combination of a logistic regression for occupancy and a Poisson regression for the number of detections).
> > >
> > > This model can easily be fitted in BUGS. Note that for this model, a single replicate is enough (there is no j). Also note that one would usually have an offset in the Poisson part of the model, to account for unequal length (of time or transect) of observation.
> > >
> > > If you can assume independence, then this seems to be a very useful model. If you don't have independence (for instance, some aggregation of detection in time or space), then this autocorrelation ought to be modelled and you must model the individual detections. One conceptually simple way of doing so is by imagining two latent processes underlying the measured detections, between which there are switches with some probability. GGA have lately developed such a 2MMPP model (a 2-state Markov-modulated point process model --- try to say this a couple of times quickly ....). She has code in Matlab, but I think not (yet) for any language that is widely spoken in ecology, such as R or BUGS.

messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] Re: manually fixing parameters?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Travis,

OK, I did not know that offsets were not allowed in colext.

On the other hand: what you want is to fix a parameter and this is not the same as using an offset. Use of an offset is for the specific case of fixing the coefficient of a continuous covariate at 1, and this is most often used in Poisson GLMs. This is not the same as when you want to fix a parameter at some other value, such as 0.

I would use PRESENCE or MARK for what you want to use.

Kind regards  --  Marc

Let me try this again.  First, to attempt to redeem myself from my wrong statements earlier.  If gamma and epsilon are to be set to psi1 and 1-psi1 (and not zero), then under that model the two years are independent (with possibly different detection probabilities).  You could then simply feed occu the data as if you had twice the number of sites (each season providing a "separate" set of sites).  You'd get the estimates and an AIC value for comparison purposes to an unrestricted model fit in colext.

But when gamma and epsilon are zero, a site cannot change status from one year to the next.  A site that is unoccupied in year 1 remains unoccupied in year 2.  Likewise, an occupied site in year 1 remains occupied in year 2.  So this model can also be estimated with occu with n sites and v = v1 + v2 visits (where v1 and v2 are the respective number of visits in years 1 and 2).  There are just 3 parameters to estimate (if there are no covariates):  psi1, p1, and p2 (where p1 and p2 are the per visit detection probabilities for years 1 and 2, respectively).

Is that closer to what you wanted?

messages.body_plain:
Dear Jim,

just one comment: most of the times one cannot compare deviances or AIC scores across different model fitting functions in unmarked (nor between different software programs in general), since the "likelihood structure" may be different.  Hence, unless Richard Chandler, Ian Fiske, or Andy Royle confirm that this is indeed possible for occu() and colext(), I would not.

So: as a test of closure, I'd simply cheat on unmarked and do that in PRESENCE or MARK, where you can fix params within the same model fitting function.

Kind regards  --- Marc

Betreff: Re: [unmarked] Re: manually fixing parameters?

Let me try this again.  First, to attempt to redeem myself from my wrong statements earlier.  If gamma and epsilon are to be set to psi1 and 1-psi1 (and not zero), then under that model the two years are independent (with possibly different detection probabilities).  You could then simply feed occu the data as if you had twice the number of sites (each season providing a "separate" set of sites).  You'd get the estimates and an AIC value for comparison purposes to an unrestricted model fit in colext.

But when gamma and epsilon are zero, a site cannot change status from one year to the next.  A site that is unoccupied in year 1 remains unoccupied in year 2.  Likewise, an occupied site in year 1 remains occupied in year 2.  So this model can also be estimated with occu with n sites and v = v1 + v2 visits (where v1 and v2 are the respective number of visits in years 1 and 2).  There are just 3 parameters to estimate (if there are no covariates):  psi1, p1, and p2 (where p1 and p2 are the per visit detection probabilities for years 1 and 2, respectively).

Is that closer to what you wanted?

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] descritizing camera data for occupancy analysis
messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] descritizing camera data for occupancy analysis
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

I'm also really pleased to see this being discussed. For years I've wondered about the ramifications of collapsing camera data arbitrarily for occupancy estimation, especially with fairly sparse carnivore datasets. After discussing this with many statisticians and researchers my take is that--within reason--the results you get should be the same regardless of encounter interval length as long as you 1) interpret estimates using the correct interval length (e.g., 1-day probability of detection if daily encounter histories, 1-week if collapsed over a week), 2) don't create histories that are too sparse or dense (i.e., all 1s), and model any obvious heterogeneity in detection probability (e.g., if you were analyzing using a 1-day interval but baiting a site every two weeks).

I currently have a student looking at this with a black bear dataset--trying various interval lengths for encounter histories and seeing what kind of estimates he gets for p and psi.

Best,

Robert

On Tuesday, January 20, 2015 at 1:59:11 PM UTC-8, Mathias Tobler wrote:
> I think the issue has been summarized really well so far but I would like to add a few things based on my experience with camera trap data and occupancy models. While correlation can be an issue on a short time scale (1-2 days) overdispersion of the data is often a bigger issue, especially for abundant species and species with small home ranges. Camera traps are often run over long periods of time (e.g. 60 to 90 days) so that you can potentially end up with a large number of detections. For some species in our dataset the number of days a species was detected at a camera can range from 1 to 35 out of 60 sampling days. This heterogeneity among cameras can lead to a poor model fit. Generally we found that the Royle-Nichols model improves fit but even then there is too much overdispersion when using one day as a sampling period. Pooling the data over 5 or 6 days helps bringing those large numbers down while little affecting the low numbers. So loosing information can be helpful. So far I had little success with modeling the overdispersion using a negative binomial or a Poisson log-normal model. Using a Poisson detection model instead of a Binomial as suggested by Marc did not affect model fit either.
>
> Overdispersion is less of an issue for carnivores with large home ranges. Those species cover large areas and spend little time near a single camera. Ungulates or smaller mammals on the other hand can can pass by a camera almost daily in some cases. Some of the differences among cameras can be addressed by covariates such as on/off trail or habitat type but we found that a lot of the variation can not be explained. It is easy to imagine that if a camera is close to an individuals home range center we would get more detections while if the camera is at the edge of a home range we get fewer detections, which is exactly what the SECR models assume. Cameras can also unintentionally be placed close to an important food source, denn, travel path etc. which increases the number of detections compared to other cameras. These detections are not necessarily correlated in time.
>
> So my suggestion would be to try to model  your data with a Royle-Nichols model with 1 day as a sampling occasion and the assess model fit. If the model does not fit then I would pool data over several days.
>
> Regards,
>
> Mathias
>
>
>
> On Monday, January 19, 2015 at 11:32:19 AM UTC-8, Murray Efford wrote:
> > I agree strongly with Andy on this - the key point being to pick a time unit that we expect for biological reasons to yield plausibly independent data. For the remaining dependence, presumably you mean a Markovian (transient) behavioural response rather than the conventional permanent one of Otis et al. Mb.
> >
> > Also, re-stating what may be already obvious and well documented: If your (nightly) observations are independent (i.e. Bernoulli trials) and you don't want to model changing detection probability over time then it is mathematically equivalent to model their aggregate as binomial (i.e. to model the sum across occasions). Can save time.
> >
> > Since I mentioned 2-MMPP: I have found a 3/4-documented R package I wrote that fits this to continuous data from multiple sites for occupancy (0/1), Poisson and negative binomial N (cf Royle and Nichols). If anyone wants this they can contact me (I won't be putting it on CRAN).
> >

> >
> > hi Robin, Marc, Murray, et al:
> >
> >  This is a really good discussion of an important issue.
> >
> >  I wanted to add my 2 cents worth on the issue of "to aggregate or not" -- I think for most camera trapping studies of carnivores it is pointless to try to model the continuous time data because often the very short term "visits" are almost completely dependent and those detections are not informative about the important parameters of the model.  e.g., a tiger will go back and forth along a trail segment 10 times in an hour or two, even a minute or two apart.  This is why I think using a nightly sample interval makes sense (and also it's a natural period of activity for most species).  Of course there is still potentially dependence from one night to the next but this is well modeled in many cases with a behavioral reponse.
> >
> >   I make the same argument in attempting to model scat detections of some species. Many carnivores use latrines or similar high density areas and the actual rate of scatting on latrines is essentially irrelevant unless you're studying behavior.

> > > I gather from this list serve (and from a cross post on the yahoo  camera trapping list serve) that a succinct answer to my question of whether there was some published recommendations is: no, not much published... except for the general recommendations to NOT descritize continuous data, both in the occupancy literature (Gurutzeta) and S(E)CR literature (Borchers et al. 2014 MEE). I suppose the best way to take this advice when still chopping up continuous data is to chop it up as fine as possible (while still considering the auto-correlation issues if possible). Your point, Marc about issues with actually being able to estimate occupancy when data is chopped up very finely is well taken; I have had issues in unmarked (the usual Hessian error) when camera data was descritize a little too finely, but that goes away when collapsing data, even just a little bit. In that way you may get rid of dependence and hence be able to use a simpler model (or do estimation at all, if you don't know how to fit the more complex model). > > > > Dear Robin,
> > > >
> > > > if you discretize and analyse using a standard occupancy model, then you typically lose information, whenever more than a single detection per occasion gets subsumed into a single '1' in the resulting history. Viewed from this angle, it would be best to discretize finely so that you never have more than a single detection per occasion. On the other hand, this may lead to very large data sets (lots of occasions) and moreover, there may be serial dependence, i.e., neighbouring occasions may not be independent samples from the underlying presence/absence process. This is a problem that you would have to deal with by adoping more complex occupancy models, see Hines et al. (tigers on trails paper, 2010) and recent follow-up paper for dynamic occupancy. These models have been implemented in PRESENCE (not sure about MARK). Note that independence or lack thereof in space (as for transect-based sampling) is very similar or identical to that in time (as for your camera-trap data).
> > > >
> > > > Some would argue that discretisation of measurements made on a continuous process is always a bad idea and that you should directly model a continuous detection process, in space or in time. This typically leads to Poisson process models, which in the context of occupancy estimation have been introduced by Gurutzeta Guillera Arroita (GGA) (papers in JABES, MEE and elsewhere). The simplest such models assumes independence in space or time. The individual detections can be aggregated into a detection frequency per transect or per camera and some total time interval, say C_i for the number of detections at trap or transect i.
> > > >
> > > > Then, you can specify the following variant of occupancy model, which has a Poisson instead of a Binomial description of the observation process:
> > > >
> > > > z_i ~ Bernoulli(psi)              # Presence/absence (z) is like a coin flip
> > > > C_i ~ Poisson(z_i * lambda_i) # lambda is detection rate, i.e., the expected number of detections given that a site is occupied.
> > > >
> > > > You can model pattern in occupancy probability by logit(psi_i) = some linear model and those in the detection frequency by log(lambda_i) = some linear model, exactly as in a GLM (this model is the combination of a logistic regression for occupancy and a Poisson regression for the number of detections).
> > > >
> > > > This model can easily be fitted in BUGS. Note that for this model, a single replicate is enough (there is no j). Also note that one would usually have an offset in the Poisson part of the model, to account for unequal length (of time or transect) of observation.
> > > >
> > > > If you can assume independence, then this seems to be a very useful model. If you don't have independence (for instance, some aggregation of detection in time or space), then this autocorrelation ought to be modelled and you must model the individual detections. One conceptually simple way of doing so is by imagining two latent processes underlying the measured detections, between which there are switches with some probability. GGA have lately developed such a 2MMPP model (a 2-state Markov-modulated point process model --- try to say this a couple of times quickly ....). She has code in Matlab, but I think not (yet) for any language that is widely spoken in ecology, such as R or BUGS.

messages.subject_clean: Organizing the unmarkedMultFrame
messages.body_plain:
Hello everybody,

Thank you in advance for your response.  I am trying to organize my data into an unmarkedMultFrame.
I can succesfully create the unmarkedMultFrame, but when I try to run a simple model, such as:
fm0 <- colext(~1, ~1, ~1, ~1, umf)
I get the following error message:
Error in data.frame(..., check.names = FALSE) :
  arguments imply differing number of rows: 1695, 0

Here is some basic info about my study:
number of sites = 91
number of visits per season = 3
number of seasons = 12

In my study, I had 91 unique sites, which I visited 3 times over the course of 6 rounds during the spring of two years 2013-2014.
I am treating each round of sampling as a separate season, so I have 12 seasons total, if I stack the data.
In my attached .csv, each row corresponds to a site, and includes a detection history that is 3 digits long, corresponding to the 3 surveys I performed at that site during that season.
I think my problem is in the obsCovs portion of the umf data frame.  If I surveyed a site during a season, I surveyed it 3 times, so I have observation level covariates (e.g. noise level at time of survey) corresponding to each of the zeroes and ones of the detection history.    However, I examined the umf data frame in R and I think it is reading each of the three ObsCovs as a separate row (1695 rows instead of 565 rows).

Here is a sample of my code:

library(unmarked)
smbdata <- read.csv("smbdata.csv", header=TRUE)

SORAy <- smbdata[,5:7]

siteCovs <- smbdata[,c(29:42)]

years <- smbdata[,c(2:4)]

obsCovs <- list(Obs=smbdata[,c(14:16)], Start=smbdata[,c(17:19)],
                Sky=smbdata[,c(20:22)], Wind=smbdata[,c(23:25)],
                Noise=smbdata[,c(26:28)])

SORA <- unmarkedMultFrame(y=SORAy,
                         siteCovs=siteCovs, yearlySiteCovs=years,
                         obsCovs=obsCovs,
                         numPrimary=12)

fm0 <- colext(~1, ~1, ~1, ~1, SORA)

Again, thank you in advance for your response.  I'm sorry if this doesn't make a lot of sense, but I'm attempting a space-for-time analysis, but I think I really have a space-AND-time situation.  In summary, my main questions are:
1) Have formatted my umf data frame correctly, given my sampling format of 3 surveys per site per season?
2) Do I need to include rows of all NAs for the sites that were not visited at all in a given round?
3) Have I correctly identified my primary and secondary sampling periods?  My current understanding is that I have 12 primary and 3 secondary.

messages.subject: Analysis Questions Regarding an Avian Abundance Study
messages.subject_clean: Analysis Questions Regarding an Avian Abundance Study
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am currently analyzing data from an avian abundance study that was conducted in Pennsylvania.  Below are some of the specifics about the study.

1) The study used 26 different sites that are located across the state of Pennsylvania.  Within each site, there were places (subsites) randomly chosen to count birds.

2) Within each subsite, birds were counted (over a 5 minute window) along with the distance they were away from the surveyor.  The distance was recorded as either being in 0-50 or 50-100 meter bins.

3) The data was collected over two years and each site was visited twice during a year.

4) Site specific covariates were collected for each visit (wind conditions, time, surveyor, etc.)

There seems to be a couple of different routes that could be taken when doing the analysis with the functions in the unmarked package.  Below I give those and my comments/questions regarding each in terms of this data set.

A) Use the gdistsamp function.

1) Would the analysis need to be done for each year separately since the population would be considered open over a two year period?

2)  Will there be estimation problems?  There are only two distance bins and two visits per year.  These are the bare minimum required for estimation (probability of detection and availability) and the counts per bin per visit are small.

3) Can the model be fit for all 26 sites at one time or would it need to be fit separately for each of the sites?

4) Does the amount of time per site (5 minutes), play a role in the model?

I have fit this model by year several times and the convergence problems are significant. When optim does converge it takes a long time to do so.

B) Using the pcountOpen function.

1) Does it make sense to reformat the data into point counts and ignore the distance bins? Will this result in a sampling design that can be used with the Dail and Madsen (2011) model? This would take care of the small number of bins and the model allows for an open population.

2) Are there any real advantages to using the distance sampling design versus the point count design, especially when there are only two distance bins?  This study will be conducted in the future and I want to help improve the study's design.

3)  Can the model be fit for all 26 sites at one time or would it need to be fit separately for each of the sites?

4) Does the amount of time per site (5 minutes), play a role in the model?

Thanks for your help,

Russ

messages.body_plain:
hi Russ,

 Yes you should use the gdistsamp function if you have distance interval data. If you have a reasonable sample size there should not be convergence problems that can't be resolved by improving starting values and so on.

1) Would the analysis need to be done for each year separately since the population would be considered open over a two year period?

no you should be able to combine both years into one model, this is what gdistsamp is good for (it fits a temporary emigration type of model). But you have 4 total periods (2 within a year) so it's unclear how to properly structure the multi-scale sampling. You might think about stacking the replicate samples within a year or among years or pooling the data from both samples within a year. There is no right answer here you'll have to think about it and try different things.

2)  Will there be estimation problems?  There are only two distance bins and two visits per year.  These are the bare minimum required for estimation (probability of detection and availability) and the counts per bin per visit are small.

I don't see any reason to expect estimation problems if you have sufficient data. If you have too small a data set then you could always have problems no matter what you do.

3) Can the model be fit for all 26 sites at one time or would it need to be fit separately for each of the sites?

I would recommend analyzing the 52 different point count locations as one big data set.

4) Does the amount of time per site (5 minutes), play a role in the model?

not as long as it was the same at all sites.

regards
andy

messages.subject: N-mixture model assumptions and camera trap data
messages.subject_clean: N-mixture model assumptions and camera trap data
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'd like to estimate the abundance of unmarked animals from camera trap data, ideally using the full information contained in the counts. This leads me to think of the N-mixture model. It seems, however, that the model assumes counts within an occasion are independent (binomial flips of N coins), which is difficult to verify with unmarked animals in camera traps - double counting is a possibility (flipping more than one coin per N). I was wondering if anyone has any experience of applying this model to camera trap data (or data from any other continuous-time detectors), or otherwise has any thoughts/advice on this issue? Would the model give negatively biased estimates of N as a result?

Advice much appreciated,
Thanks
Ollie

messages.body_plain:
hi Ollie,
 I think it would almost certainly give positively biased estimates of N in this case.
 I'm sure some of our users have looked into this so I hope some people offer up their experiences.

 In the case where individuals can be counted multiple times there are other types of models that you might consider such as Poisson/Poisson mixtures instead of Binomial/Poisson mixtures.
 A specific model has that N[site] ~ Poisson and then the number of detections of each individual is also Poisson (which allows > 1 capture per individual).

 You would have to write code for this model yourself or else use BUGS. Someday perhaps we will put such models in unmarked.

regards
andy

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ollie
I'm afraid my jaundiced view extends to Royle/Nichols (there was some stuff on this in our 2012 Ecoscience paper, and some simulations). There are two problems (i) there is no N, at least none that is adequately defined independently of the sampling process, and (ii) if there was an N, p would often be highly heterogeneous among individuals, causing all sorts of bias. (And there is probably a third one in your case of overdispersion, but that can be fixed). I don't think random detector placement changes much.
Be warned I seem to belong to a small minority.
Murray

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,
 Of course I mostly disagree with Murray on his two main points: (1)  incremental improvements that address small details are worth achieving and , indeed, just about everything we or anyone will ever do their whole lives amounts only to incremental improvements. So if you can string a few incremental improvements together to solve a problem you're probably doing ok. (2) On the imprecision definition of N:  Some models ought to be preferred on the grounds that they are better descriptions of reality than others. So in the case of point counts of birds we know, as a matter of fact, that local population size in the vicinity of a point varies among points and it must lead to heterogeneity in detection. It can't be any other way.  So of course trying to accommodate that in logistic regression type models (as in the RN model) or Poisson regression (as in the N-mixture model) is preferable to pretending that it is an additive normal random effect (which never actually exists in nature).

 I do agree that N is not well defined in such cases, most of the time but what exactly is the argument that this has relevance to? That one should not model things? Or that one should use a normal random effects model? or that one should do .... what exactly? Ultimately, of course, we can improve on the models by making them spatially explicit (see Chandler and Royle, 2013, AOAS and a forthcoming paper by David Ramsey in JWM).
 Incremental improvements!

regards,
andy

Rhetoric on incremental improvement doesn't seem to get us very far without some measure of what has improved. Murray

hi Russ,

 your data set looks sufficient to me, I think you should have no trouble fitting models to this.
 the gdistsamp function does take a long time because it's marginalizing over the prior distribution for N by doing the summation (whereas the distsamp function takes advantage of an analytic result to avoid having to do that).

 (2) right, by "stacking"  I mean treating replicates as new sites. I agree this would probably lead to ignoring some dependence but I don't think that is really critical. (might be worth doing a small simulation study to see the effects)

regards
andy

Thanks Again,

Russ

messages.body_plain:
Dear Russ,

re. your questions, it is best if you think of a hierarchical model as the hierarchical distance sampling model as simply a complex kind of generalized linear model (GLM): inside, there is always some linear modeling of covariate effects happening. So (almost .... exactly ....) everything is *just* like with lm() or glm() when you want to express variability in some response by variability of some explanatory variables.

Therefore,
(1) if you think it's not linear, then you can add a quadratic term of time of day. Remember that the modeling in a GLM takes place on the link-transformed scale, so while the model is linear mathematically, it is not usually represented by a straight line (for a continuous covariate). --- You might also break a continuous covariate into classes, effectively making it a factor, to accommodate possible non-linearity.
(2) Usually you would think that, say, April 1 in year 1 is pretty similar to April 1 in year 2; hence, I would start numbering anew.

Kind regards  --- Marc

messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I have a question regarding the utility of using individual detection rates, meaning those from mark-recapture studies, within an occupancy modeling framework.  What I have is an extensive camera trap array and, within a small subset of the area covered by the array, I’ll have uniquely marked individuals.  Thus, I should be able to estimate an individual detection probability using either a mark-resight model or with proximity sensors we will have on the radio-collars and the cameras.  So my question is, what would be the best way to incorporate this individual detection probability, estimated from a only a subset of my broader camera array, when looking at the camera trap data from the rest of the array in which there are no uniquely marked individuals?  It would seem as though having p-hat in this sense would somehow allow me to scale occupancy based estimates of site detection probabilities into actual abundance or density.  Any suggestions would be greatly appreciated.

Shawn
